prompt: Explain inflation using only tailgating metaphors. Do not stop when the metaphors break down.
response:
Alright, let’s do this. You’re on the highway. The big game just ended.

Inflation is when everyone leaves the stadium at the exact same time.

Suddenly, every single car is trying to merge onto the same highway. There are way too many cars for the number of lanes. That’s too much money chasing too few goods. The highway is the economy. The cars are dollars.

The central bank, the Fed, is the state trooper. Their job is to set the speed limit—that’s the interest rate. When the trooper sets the speed limit at “parking lot,” money is cheap. Everyone floors it, zig-zagging between lanes, because borrowing is free and everyone’s tank is full of easy credit. The highway gets packed. Bumper to bumper. A fender bender in the tech sector causes a pileup, but nobody cares because everyone’s still trying to get to the off-ramp for used cars and houses.

Prices are the gap between cars. When the highway is empty, you can drive like a maniac and nobody cares. You’ve got space. That’s stable prices. But when inflation hits, everyone tailgates everyone else. The gap closes. A dollar that used to get you a safe following distance of three car lengths now gets you six inches from the guy’s bumper. Your dollar doesn’t go as far. You’re white-knuckling it just to maintain the same speed.

Now you’re the guy in the F-150 riding my ass because you think I’m going too slow, but I’m already doing 80. That’s demand-pull inflation. You’re demanding I go faster, so I speed up to avoid getting hit, but then the guy in front of me speeds up, and suddenly the whole highway is doing 95, a death wish of rising wages and prices chasing each other. You’re not getting there any faster; you’re just increasing the risk of a catastrophic crash.

Then there’s the semi-truck that cuts across all four lanes and drops its load of microchips and lumber. That’s a supply shock. The lanes are closed.
